title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

items.title: Sandworm and Qilin are inside Cisco firewall management: a critical auth bypass, exploited since August
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 — a critical authentication bypass in Secure Firewall Management Center, patched back in March — has been exploited since August. Crafted HTTP requests reach a process created at boot and hand an unauthenticated attacker root on the appliance that configures your firewalls. Cisco Talos attributes three activity clusters: one deploying a web shell to harvest credentials, one tied to the Russian state group Sandworm delivering Cyclops Blink, and one linked to Qilin ransomware staging encryption target lists. CISA added the flaw to KEV with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September — today. For OT defenders the significance is not the firewall — it is the management plane above it. Whoever holds FMC holds the rule set separating enterprise from plant, and can rewrite it without touching a single controller.

items.title: An AI-run campaign compromised 440 print servers in weeks — and the interesting number is how few of them needed a human
items.content_text: GreyNoise published research on 11 September describing a Russian-speaking actor who built and tested exploits for two PaperCut NG/MF flaws in a private lab, then handed the campaign itself to AI agents. The result was 440 compromised deployments across 395 identified organisations in 48 countries. Education took the largest share at 204, but manufacturing and utilities are named among the affected sectors, alongside retail, professional services, IT and managed service providers. The mechanics are ordinary post-exploitation — LSASS and registry credential harvesting on domain-joined hosts, NoPac against unpatched domain controllers, a new Domain Admins account where the host was itself a DC. What is not ordinary is the pace: GreyNoise reports some environments falling in minutes or seconds. Credentials were harvested from 280 hosts, secrets exfiltrated from 137, and domain admin reached in 12. The relevance to a plant is the domain, not the printer.

items.title: Boston Scientific closes it out: manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping fully restored — and no evidence the production systems were ever compromised
items.content_text: The operational story is now closed; the cost is not. On 9 September the company said manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping are fully restored and running at or above normal levels, ending the disruption first identified on 25 August. Independent assessment by CrowdStrike and other third-party experts found no evidence of ongoing threat activity and no evidence that product-development systems, manufacturing systems or cloud platforms were compromised; remote cardiac-device monitoring, which had also been disrupted, is restored as well. Unauthorised access remains assessed as limited to internal-facing IT. What does not reverse is the 8 September securities filing: the company no longer expects to meet the third-quarter and full-year sales-growth and adjusted-EPS ranges it issued in July, expects to recapture only some of the lost revenue as it works down backlog, and has deferred a revised outlook to the 28 October earnings call. No ransomware group has been named and no root cause has been disclosed. Nothing touched a control system, and roughly a fortnight of output is gone anyway.

items.title: The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
items.content_text: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register.

items.title: The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
items.content_text: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear.

items.title: A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
items.content_text: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable.

items.title: A Bavarian municipal utility was encrypted a week ago and kept the lights and water on — the separation held, the office did not
items.content_text: Stadtwerke Landsberg, the city-owned utility for Landsberg am Lech, told customers on Monday that attackers encrypted its central IT network in an incident that began overnight on 1 September. The operator says electricity, water and its other essential services were never affected; office systems were, and staff remain reachable only intermittently by phone and email while external specialists complete a forensic investigation. No ransomware brand has been named and the utility has not said whether an extortion demand followed. It cannot yet rule out that customer data — names, addresses, contact details and bank details — was accessed. A comparable attack on the utility serving Kamen, Bönen and Bergkamen in North Rhine-Westphalia disrupted internal systems for weeks in late June. For OT defenders the useful detail is the one that did not make the headline: a small municipal multi-utility lost its business systems and still ran supply, which is the outcome segmentation is supposed to produce and the one worth confirming you could reproduce.

items.title: A five-week-old ransomware brand ships an ESXi build — and its two best-known victims are a kitchen maker and a telecoms engineering firm
items.content_text: Panzer surfaced in August as a ransomware-as-a-service operation and, inside its first month, listed victims in eleven countries, among them two Italian companies: Doimo Cucine, a designer-kitchen manufacturer near Treviso, posted on 17 August with 30 GB claimed, and NTE Italia, a telecommunications engineering consultancy in Catanzaro, posted four days later with 16 GB claimed. Neither has confirmed anything, and no encryptor sample or network indicator has been published, so the technical picture is thin. What is not thin is the commercial scaffolding: an affiliate dashboard reached through a screened Tox application, an 80/20 revenue split, and builds for Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and VMware ESXi. The ESXi target is the part that matters to a plant. Historians, MES, batch servers, engineering VMs and the jump hosts into the control network usually share a handful of hypervisors, so one compromised management interface encrypts the entire Level 3 estate in a single action — and the plant keeps running blind until it cannot.

items.title: Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
items.content_text: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier.

items.title: A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC.

items.title: The quartermaster model: US authorities seize the platforms a China-nexus group used to scan power companies, telecoms and a water district
items.content_text: The FBI and Justice Department have seized domains behind QTFY, a state-backed Chinese operation that ran two platforms — QScan for reconnaissance and QTRouter for traffic relay — across a campaign lasting years. Court records name telecommunications firms, hospitals, defence contractors, power companies and financial institutions among the critical-infrastructure targets, alongside federal agencies including the Department of Energy. QScan infected thousands of internet-of-things devices worldwide and enrolled them into the QTRouter relay network, alongside leased proxies and virtual private servers, which is what kept the operation’s origin hidden for years. The NSA and FBI say the operators used zero-day and n-day flaws for initial access, then stole legitimate credentials for persistence — a Check Point Quantum Gateway flaw to scan power and telecommunications firms, Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance zero-days against DOE and health research labs, and a BeyondTrust flaw against a US state government, with a water district also targeted. Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, which tracked the group for years and supported the takedown, describe a “quartermaster model”: reconnaissance, proxy orchestration and operational routing run as one service, sold on to the People’s Liberation Army and the Ministry of State Security. The relevance for OT is the shape rather than the victim list — the edge and IoT estate that most operators do not inventory was both the target set and the infrastructure. It stays on the page a fortnight on because the seizure removed the platforms, not the method: the same unowned edge estate is still the way in.
tags: DOJ/FBI takedown and NSA/FBI advisory — QTFY, a China-nexus scanning and proxy operation against US critical infrastructure

items.title: CISA reissues its insider-threat playbook — and the worked example is an automation engineer walking out with the source code
items.content_text: CISA published an updated Insider Threat Mitigation Guide on 10 September, aimed at critical-infrastructure owners and operators and written to scale from a two-person utility upward. The case it leads with is pointedly industrial: a US energy technology company whose head of automation engineering copied proprietary source code for a foreign competitor, with authorities later estimating that a fifth of the competitor’s global installed product ran on the stolen software. The victim lost more than a billion dollars in shareholder equity and close to 700 jobs; the 2018 trade-secret judgment came to $59 million. The framework itself is unglamorous — define, detect, assess, manage, improve — run by a multidisciplinary team against a written incident-response plan and a low/medium/high risk rubric, with anonymous reporting channels and retaliation protection because the recurring failure is a colleague who noticed and said nothing. It earns a place on an OT page for a reason most insider programmes miss: in a plant, the person with the engineering-workstation password, the controller protection-level passwords and physical access to the panel is the same person, and none of the network controls elsewhere on this page constrain them.

items.title: September’s ICS Patch Tuesday reaches the safety controller: a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Schneider’s Modicon M580
items.content_text: Schneider Electric, Siemens and Aveva published their September advisories on 8 September, and the one that matters most sits inside a controller family run on safety duty. CVE-2026-3869, rated CVSS 9.2, is an authentication weakness in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety ranges — the mid-tier PLC that runs a great many water, power and process plants, and the same hardware many sites rely on for safety functions. Schneider also fixed high-severity defects in PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, and finally shipped Modicon MC80 patches for weaknesses first disclosed as far back as 2019. Siemens added four critical advisories, including the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay. CISA followed on 10 September with ICSA-26-253-01, the formal advisory for the Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor flaws, which is the only new ICS advisory it published in the last two days. Nothing here is exploited. What makes it consequential is where it lands: on the devices whose failure mode is physical, not informational — and on a patch clock measured in validated outages rather than days.

items.title: The other remote-access box just went live: public exploit code for a NetScaler auth bypass, and attacks the same week
items.content_text: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 on 19 August — an authentication bypass, CVSS 9.3, in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server, with SAML configurations among those affected. For a fortnight it stayed theoretical. Then public exploit code appeared in early September, and on 3 September sensor operators began recording bypass attempts from multiple source addresses across four countries, with reporting on 4 September confirming attackers had turned to the flaw in the wild. NetScaler is not an OT product, but it is very often the thing an engineer authenticates through before reaching a jump host, a historian or a vendor session — which makes an unauthenticated bypass on it a route to the plant, not merely to the corporate estate.

items.title: CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
items.content_text: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design.

items.title: CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window.

items.title: A fourth boundary box in a fortnight: a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the platform your outsourced IT uses to reach every machine you own
items.content_text: N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218 on 6 September and rated it CVSS 10.0 — an unauthenticated attacker can execute code on an internet-exposed N-central server, in a low-complexity attack requiring no credentials and no user interaction. The fix is N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4, build 2026.3.1.14, and reporting notes it is the fourth N-central hotfix in roughly five weeks. Huntress reported a compromised production environment but could not establish which of the disclosed flaws was used, and flagged this one as a possible zero-day alongside two high-severity issues; N-able’s own notice describes exploitation observed in the wild. The Shadowserver Foundation tracks close to 1,500 internet-exposed N-central servers, most in the United States and Europe. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform — an agent with system-level rights on every endpoint it manages. For industrial sites, the question is whether the managed service provider that patches your engineering workstations, historians and plant IT runs one, and whether their console is reachable from the internet.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits.

items.title: Microsoft ships its largest patch day on record, and the two flaws already being used are both local privilege escalation
items.content_text: Microsoft’s September release closes roughly 973 vulnerabilities — the largest single Patch Tuesday it has published — with about 113 rated critical. Two are confirmed exploited in the wild, and both matter more to OT than their scores suggest. CVE-2026-81963 is an improper link-resolution flaw in the Windows Update Stack that lets a local attacker escalate to SYSTEM; it is reported as the first Windows Update Stack defect exploited as a zero-day. CVE-2026-85880 is a privilege-escalation flaw in Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call, rated CVSS 7.8, also giving SYSTEM. CISA added both to the KEV catalogue on 8 September with a 22 September federal remediation deadline. Neither is remotely exploitable on its own, which is precisely why they pair badly with the boundary devices elsewhere on this page: the exploited edge appliances supply the initial foothold, and these supply the jump to SYSTEM on the Windows host that host sits next to. In a plant that host is usually an HMI, an engineering workstation or a historian — machines that are rarely on a monthly patch cadence and often cannot be rebooted on demand. Two further items drew attention but are not confirmed exploited: CVE-2026-69829, a Windows Shell remote-code-execution flaw rated CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-69730 in Windows DNS, assessed as likely exploitable.

items.title: The free assessment most small operators actually used has been withdrawn — the tool survives, the adviser who ran it does not
items.content_text: CISA has confirmed that its regional staff will stop delivering six no-cost assessments offered to critical-infrastructure operators: Cyber Resilience Reviews, Cyber Resilience Essentials surveys, Ransomware Readiness Assessments, Incident Management Reviews, External Dependencies Management Assessments and Cyber Infrastructure Surveys. All six were run on site by a regional adviser using the Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) to produce a prioritised improvement report. In its statement the agency described the change as retiring legacy questionnaire assessments to reduce duplication, and said operators will be pointed instead to the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals. CSET itself remains open source, though the current release disables the retired assessment modules; older versions still run them, without an adviser to interpret the output. Field staff were told to stop at a 25 August internal meeting. The reporting notes the change lands amid a roughly one-third reduction in CISA’s workforce over the past year.

items.title: The clock started yesterday: anyone selling a connected product into the EU now owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. As of yesterday, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process.

items.title: DOE opens the comment window on foreign-supplied grid equipment — and asks operators to define “remote access” for it
items.content_text: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response published a request for information in today’s Federal Register to inform how it implements the bulk-power-system executive order covering foreign-supplied equipment, which the notice cites as Executive Order 14421. The questions are the ones that decide whether the eventual rule is workable: what transactions should fall inside scope, how supply-chain risk should be assessed, and how to treat software and firmware, digital and maintenance services, and remote access. That last item is where asset owners have the most to contribute and the most to lose by staying quiet — vendor remote access into a substation is not one thing, and a definition written without operators in the room tends to capture routine relay-setting support and firmware delivery alongside the cases the order is actually aimed at. This is an RFI, not a rule or a directive: nothing is prohibited, no filing is required and no equipment becomes non-compliant today. Comments are due 9 October 2026, which gives utilities, co-ops, integrators and OEMs a month to respond.
